Welcome toDrawing Microstates

Hold a small system at fixed temperature — which energies do drawn microstates take?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: microstates of a small system drawn at a fixed temperature

Source

Concept
A small system in contact with a large reservoir at temperature T: the Boltzmann factor e−E/kBT of each microstate, the density of states g(E) ∝ Ea with a = f/2 − 1, and the distribution of energies of microstates drawn at random.
Serves
Comparing the single most probable microstate with the energy at which the system is most likely to be found, and how that energy depends on T and on the way g(E) rises.
Inquiry
Five questions and a closing summary card. The student sets T (150–300 K) and the system (f = 2, 3, 4 or 6 momentum components), presses Draw microstates, and reads the histogram, the tick strip and the Readouts panel below the controls.
Misconception
Whether the probability of one microstate and the probability of an energy are the same thing — examined through the draws, not stated on screen.
How it is measured
Each draw takes f momentum components from Gaussian distributions (Box–Muller), so E = (kBT/2)(Z₁² + … + Zf²); 4000 draws at 500 per second; bins 2 meV wide, bar height = fraction of draws in the bin ÷ 2 meV. The ticks sit at Ek = 160 meV × (k/60)1/(a+1), so each gap holds the same number of microstates, and each tick's opacity is e−Ek/kBT. The g, Boltzmann and P(E) curves use separate vertical scales, the P(E) scale fixed for each system. kB = 0.08617 meV/K. Changing T or the system clears the histogram.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honours it
Commit before the revealEach question is answered before its histogram is drawn and then checked in the sim; the blue P(E) curve and the Emax readout stay hidden until the first complete draw.
Depict the lecture figureg(E), the Boltzmann factor and the microstate tick strip share one E axis, exactly as in the figure, so the histogram builds up on top of the picture it explains.
Operational quantitieskBT, the share of draws below 2 meV and Emax are read from the Readouts panel, in meV and per cent.
Stable scalesThe E axis is fixed at 0–160 meV and the P(E) scale is fixed for each system, so moving T visibly shifts and lowers the peak instead of being re-fitted away.
Exact physicsMicrostates are sampled exactly from Gaussian momentum components, not read off a drawn curve; the histogram is an independent check of P(E).
Misconception handled structurallyPlausible wrong ideas appear only as answer options, each with its own feedback, never as standing text on the screen.
Drawing Microstates at a Fixed Temperature
✦Teach me
Microstates drawn at a fixed temperature

Guided Inquiry

1 · One atom in a box

Keep one atom in a box at T = 200 K. On the strip beneath the axis the tick at E = 0, the lowest-energy microstate, is the darkest of all. Press Draw microstates and watch the histogram build up. Where do the energies of the drawn microstates pile up?

2 · The ticks near zero

Keep the same settings and look at the ticks near E = 0: after the ground state, the next tick is at 10.4 meV. Why do so few of the draws land below 2 meV, although every microstate there has the largest Boltzmann factor?

3 · One atom on a surface

Keep T = 200 K and switch to one atom on a surface, whose density of states is flat. Press Draw microstates. Where is the histogram tallest now, and what share of the draws lies below 2 meV?

4 · Doubling the temperature

Switch to two atoms in a box and set T = 150 K. Press Draw microstates and read Emax, which is 25.9 meV. Then set T = 300 K and draw again. What happens to Emax?

5 · Four systems at one temperature

Set T = 200 K, where kBT reads 17.2 meV. Step through the four systems, pressing Draw microstates each time, and read Emax: 0, 8.6, 17.2 and 34.5 meV for g flat, √E, E and E². What decides where the peak lies?

6 · One microstate against one energy

At a fixed temperature the single most probable microstate is always the lowest-energy one, since its Boltzmann factor e−E/kBT is largest. But the energy at which the system is most likely to be found is set by a product: that factor times the number of microstates at the energy, g(E).

With g ∝ Ea the product peaks at Emax = a kBT, which grows in proportion to T and with how fast g rises. Only when g is flat is the most probable energy the lowest one.

The Physics

Drawing Microstates at a Fixed Temperature · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A small system, one or two atoms, is in contact with a large reservoir at temperature T. This sim draws its microstates at random, thousands at a time, and builds up a histogram of their energies E.

What you'll learn

  • How the Boltzmann factor weights a single microstate.
  • How the density of states g(E) counts the microstates in a slice of energy.
  • How the probability of an energy P(E) is built from the two, and what fixes its peak Emax.
  • How Emax depends on the temperature T and on the system.
The set-up: a small system in thermal contact with a reservoir that holds it at temperature T.

What's on screen

  • Histogram: the energies of the microstates drawn so far, in 2 meV bins.
  • Solid curve g: the density of states. Dashed curve e−E/kBT: the Boltzmann factor. Blue curve: their product, P(E), with a dashed line at its peak, Emax. Each curve has its own vertical scale, as in the notes' Figure 30.
  • Strip of ticks under the axis: sixty microstates, one per tick, shaded by their Boltzmann factor.
  • Readouts: T, kBT, the number drawn, the share below 2 meV, and Emax.
See itDraw 4000 microstates with your current settings. Watch for: the bars of the histogram growing along the energy axis, and Drawn so far counting up to 4000.

03

Each microstate has a Boltzmann factor

A system held at temperature T is found in a particular microstate of energy E with a probability proportional to the Boltzmann factor e−E/kBT. The notes write it e−βE, with β = 1/kBT. The factor is 1 at E = 0 and smaller at every higher energy, so the single most probable microstate is always the one of lowest energy.

kBT sets how fast it falls. At 200 K, kBT = 17.2 meV: the factor drops by a factor e for every 17.2 meV, and by 100 meV it is 0.003. Dividing by Z, the sum of the factors over all microstates, makes the probabilities add to 1.

The sim shows the factor as the dashed curve, and shades each tick of its strip by it: the tick at E = 0 is the darkest.

See itDraw one atom in a box at 200 K. Watch for: the dashed curve starting at its highest on the left and falling away, with kBT = 17.2 meV in the readouts.
04

P(E) is g(E) times the Boltzmann factor

Energies are not equally crowded with microstates. If g(E) dE microstates lie between E and E + dE, the probability of finding the system in that slice is the notes' (4.50), and Z makes the area under P(E) equal to 1.

Notes (4.50).
One atom in a box, f = 3, at 200 K. Each curve has its own vertical scale, as in the notes' Figure 30.

Here g rises as √E while the Boltzmann factor falls, so their product is small at both ends and has a peak between them, at Emax = 8.6 meV. The sim draws its microstates fairly: each momentum component comes from its own Boltzmann (Gaussian) distribution, with no bias towards any energy. The histogram then builds up along the blue curve.

See itDraw 4000 microstates for one atom in a box at 200 K. Watch for: the bars piling up along the blue curve, with the peak of P(E) reading 8.6 meV.
05

Few microstates lie near E = 0

For an atom in a box g ∝ √E, which is zero at E = 0 and grows slowly. The sim's tick strip shows this: its ticks are spaced equally in number of microstates, so a wide gap means few of them. After the one at E = 0, the next tick is at 10.4 meV.

Sixty microstates at 200 K, one per tick, shaded by the Boltzmann factor. Wide gaps hold few microstates.

Each microstate near zero has the largest Boltzmann factor, but a slice there holds hardly any, so only 2.8% of the probability lies below 2 meV (the draws read about 3%).

On a surface, f = 2, g is flat and nothing offsets the Boltzmann factor. The ticks are 2.7 meV apart, P(E) is tallest at E = 0, and 1 − e−2/kBT = 11% of the probability lies below 2 meV at 200 K.

See itDraw one atom on a surface at 200 K. Watch for: the bars tallest in the lowest bin and falling steadily, with Share below 2 meV near 11%.
06

The peak sits at a kBT

For g ∝ Ea, with a = f/2 − 1, the product is Eae−E/kBT. Its peak is where the fractional rise of g, a/E, just matches the fractional fall of the Boltzmann factor, 1/kBT.

The peak of P(E).

At 200 K, kBT = 17.2 meV, and the four systems peak at 0, 8.6, 17.2 and 34.5 meV. For f = 2, a = 0: there is no peak away from zero. The mean energy is a different quantity, (a + 1)kBT = (f/2)kBT; for one atom in a box it is 25.9 meV, beyond the peak, because of the long tail.

P(E) for the four systems at 200 K, on one vertical scale; each has unit area.
See itDraw two atoms in a box at 200 K. Watch for: the peak of P(E) reading 34.5 meV, twice kBT = 17.2 meV.
See itDraw with your own T and system. Watch for: the peak of P(E) reading a × kBT, the number in the panel above.
07

Doubling T doubles the peak, and halves its height

Emax = a kBT is proportional to T. For two atoms in a box, a = 2, it moves from 25.9 meV at 150 K to 51.7 meV at 300 K.

Two atoms in a box, f = 6, at 150 K and 300 K, on one vertical scale.

P(E) keeps unit area. Spread over twice the range, its peak falls to half the height, whatever the system, since P(Emax) ∝ 1/kBT. The histogram comes out broader and lower.

A flat g does not move: for f = 2 the peak stays at zero at every temperature, and only the tail stretches.

See itDraw two atoms in a box at 150 K. Watch for: the peak of P(E) reading 25.9 meV.
See itDraw the same system at 300 K. Watch for: the peak of P(E) reading 51.7 meV, with the histogram broader and lower than at 150 K.
08

Where it matters

  • Speeds in a gas. The notes' Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution (Section 4.4) is this sim's atom in a box: the factor v2 comes from counting states in a shell, and the exponential from the Boltzmann factor, so the distribution vanishes at v = 0 and falls away at large v.
  • Thermally activated processes. The share of a distribution far out in the tail falls as e−E/kBT times a power of E. That is why a small rise in T can raise a reaction rate a lot.
  • Any system with many levels. Wherever g(E) rises and the Boltzmann factor falls, the most probable energy is set by the product, not by the lowest level.
Go deeper: the peak speed and the peak energy differ

For one atom, E = ½mv2, and the speed distribution peaks at E = kBT. The sim's P(E) for the same atom peaks at kBT/2. Both are right: P(E) dE and f(v) dv count the same atoms in slices of different widths, since dE = mv dv, so the two densities peak at different places.

09

Summary

In one line. The sim draws microstates of a small system at a fixed temperature and histograms their energies, with g(E) and the Boltzmann factor on the same axis.

Key points

  • The most probable microstate has the lowest energy; the most probable energy is set by g(E)e−E/kBT.
  • For g ∝ Ea, with a = f/2 − 1, the peak is at Emax = a kBT; for a flat g it is at zero.
  • Emax grows in proportion to T, and the peak height falls as 1/T.

Common mix-ups

  • “The draws pile up at the darkest tick.” That tick is one microstate. For an atom in a box the histogram peaks at 8.6 meV, with only about 3% of the draws below 2 meV.
  • “A flat g still peaks away from zero.” It does not. On a surface the histogram is tallest in the lowest bin, with 11% of the draws below 2 meV at 200 K.
  • “Doubling T doubles every feature.” Emax doubles, from 25.9 to 51.7 meV for two atoms in a box, but the peak height halves, because the area stays 1.

Things to try on your own

  • Draw one atom in a box at 150, 200 and 300 K. Check that Emax is half of kBT each time.
  • At 200 K, draw two atoms on a surface, f = 4. Check that Emax equals kBT.
  • Predict which system has the smallest share below 2 meV at 200 K, then draw each.
